title: Normal Variations of the Areola and Montgomery Glands: Anatomy, Physiology, and Clinical Significance

Introduction

Have you ever looked at your breasts and wondered:

“Are my areolas too big?”
“Why are there little bumps around my nipples?”
“Why are my areolas darker than someone else's?”
“Is it normal to have hair around the nipple?”

The answer to many of these questions is surprisingly simple: breasts naturally vary enormously from person to person.

The nipple–areola complex is a highly specialized part of the breast containing the nipple, areola, sensory nerves, smooth muscle, glands and other structures that work together during breastfeeding and protect the delicate skin of the area.

One particularly interesting feature is the presence of Montgomery glands, which can appear as small bumps around the areola. These glands produce an oily secretion that helps protect and lubricate the nipple–areola complex, particularly during breastfeeding.

The size, color and shape of the areola and the number and visibility of Montgomery glands can vary significantly between individuals. Pregnancy, puberty, hormonal changes, breastfeeding and aging can also change their appearance.

Most of these differences are completely normal.

However, some nipple and areolar changes — particularly new, persistent or one-sided changes — can sometimes indicate an underlying breast condition and should be evaluated.

So, what exactly are Montgomery glands? Why do some people have many visible bumps while others have only a few? And which breast changes are considered normal?

Let's take a closer look.

What Is the Areola?

The areola is the darker circular area of skin surrounding the nipple.

It is part of the nipple–areola complex (NAC) and contains several specialized structures, including:

Pigment-producing melanocytes
Sensory nerve endings
Smooth muscle fibers
Sebaceous glands
Sweat glands
Montgomery glands
Connective tissue

The areola is not simply a patch of darker skin.

It is a specialized anatomical region that helps protect the nipple and plays an important role in breastfeeding.

What Are Montgomery Glands?

Montgomery glands are specialized glands located within the areola.

They are sometimes called areolar glands.

One of the most common misconceptions is that the small bumps visible around the nipple are the glands themselves.

More accurately, the bumps are called Montgomery tubercles and represent the visible raised portions associated with the underlying Montgomery glands.

These glands are modified sebaceous glands that produce a lipid-rich secretion.

This secretion helps:

Lubricate the nipple
Maintain skin moisture
Protect the nipple from excessive dryness
Reduce cracking and irritation
Support the health of the nipple–areola skin

They become particularly noticeable in many people during pregnancy and breastfeeding because of hormonal changes.

Why Do I Have Small Bumps Around My Nipple?

Those tiny bumps around the areola are usually Montgomery tubercles.

They are a normal anatomical feature.

Some people have only a few visible bumps, while others may have many.

Their appearance can change depending on:

Puberty
Menstrual hormonal changes
Pregnancy
Breastfeeding
Temperature
Hormonal fluctuations
Individual anatomy

There is therefore no single “normal” number or appearance of these bumps.

Having many visible Montgomery tubercles does not mean something is wrong, and having very few visible ones does not mean that the glands are absent or not functioning.

How Many Montgomery Glands Are Normal?

The number of Montgomery glands varies considerably between individuals.

Anatomical studies have reported approximately 4 to 28 glands per breast, although estimates can vary depending on how the glands are identified and counted.

This wide range helps explain why some people have only a few visible bumps while others have numerous bumps around the areola.

So, if you have noticed that someone else's areolas look completely different from yours, that is not necessarily a cause for concern.

There is considerable normal variation in breast anatomy.

What Do Montgomery Glands Do?

Montgomery glands have several important functions.

1. They lubricate the nipple

Their oily secretion helps keep the skin of the nipple and areola moisturized.

This becomes particularly important during breastfeeding, when repeated infant suckling can place considerable mechanical stress on the nipple.

2. They help protect the skin

The lipid-rich secretion helps maintain the skin barrier and may reduce dryness and cracking.

3. They may have antimicrobial effects

Montgomery gland secretions contain substances that may help limit microbial growth on the nipple–areola surface.

This is particularly relevant during breastfeeding, when the nipple is repeatedly exposed to the baby's mouth and the surrounding environment.

4. They may help newborns locate the breast

Research suggests that compounds released by Montgomery glands may provide odor cues that help newborn babies orient toward the breast.

In other words, these glands may play a subtle role in helping a newborn find and attach to the breast. (pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov)

Do Montgomery Glands Help With Breastfeeding?

Yes, they appear to have several supportive roles during breastfeeding.

The secretions help maintain the condition of the nipple–areola skin and may provide sensory and olfactory cues that support newborn feeding behavior.

However, Montgomery glands are not responsible for producing breast milk.

Milk is produced by the mammary glands deeper within the breast.

Successful breastfeeding depends on several factors, including:

Adequate mammary gland development
Prolactin-driven milk production
Oxytocin-mediated milk ejection
Effective infant latch
Regular and effective milk removal

Therefore, having larger or more visible Montgomery tubercles does not mean that someone will produce more breast milk.

Does Areola Size Affect Breast Milk Production?

No.

There is a great deal of natural variation in areolar size.

Some people have relatively small areolas, while others have large areolas that cover a substantial portion of the breast.

This does not determine how much milk the breast can produce.

Milk production is primarily related to the function of the mammary gland and the hormonal and mechanical processes involved in lactation.

Similarly, having a darker or lighter areola does not determine breastfeeding ability.

Why Do Areolas Become Darker During Pregnancy?

Many people notice that their nipples and areolas become darker or more prominent during pregnancy.

This is related to hormonal changes that occur during pregnancy and increased pigmentation of the skin.

The precise biological purpose of this increased pigmentation is not completely established.

One theory is that increased contrast between the areola and surrounding breast skin may make the nipple easier for a newborn to visually identify.

However, this explanation remains an area of scientific interest rather than a proven requirement for successful breastfeeding.

After pregnancy and breastfeeding, pigmentation may gradually become lighter again, although it may not always return completely to its previous appearance.

Why Does the Size of the Areola Vary So Much?

Areolar size and shape are influenced by many factors, including:

Genetics
Hormonal changes
Puberty
Pregnancy
Breastfeeding
Age
Overall breast size
Individual body characteristics

There is therefore no ideal areola size.

Large, small, round, oval, darker, lighter, symmetrical or slightly asymmetrical areolas can all be normal.

Is It Normal for One Areola to Be Different From the Other?

Yes.

Human bodies are rarely perfectly symmetrical.

It is normal for one breast to be slightly larger than the other, and the same can apply to:

Nipple position
Areola size
Areola shape
Pigmentation
Nipple projection

Mild asymmetry that has been present for a long time is generally not concerning.

However, a new and noticeable change in one breast or nipple deserves attention, particularly if it develops suddenly or progresses over time.

Is Hair Around the Nipple Normal?

Yes.

Although hair follicles are generally absent from the nipple itself, hair can normally grow in the surrounding areolar skin.

A few fine or even darker hairs around the edge of the areola are common, particularly after puberty.

Hormonal changes can make these hairs more noticeable.

Occasional hair around the areola is therefore not usually a sign of disease.

However, if there is sudden excessive hair growth accompanied by other symptoms of hormonal imbalance, it may be worth discussing with a doctor.

Can I Remove Hair From Around My Areola?

If you choose to remove areolar hair, gentle methods are generally preferable.

Options may include:

Carefully trimming the hair
Gentle tweezing
Other appropriate hair-removal methods

The skin around the nipple is sensitive, so aggressive shaving, waxing or chemical hair-removal products can cause irritation.

Avoid picking or squeezing the Montgomery glands themselves.

Should You Squeeze Montgomery Glands?

No.

Montgomery tubercles are normal anatomical structures and generally do not need to be emptied or “cleaned.”

Squeezing them can cause:

Irritation
Inflammation
Infection
Skin injury
Pain

If one of the bumps becomes unusually swollen, painful, red, or produces pus, it should be evaluated rather than repeatedly squeezed.

Can Montgomery Glands Get Blocked?

Yes, although this is not usually a serious problem.

A Montgomery gland can occasionally become blocked, producing a small, swollen, or pimple-like bump.

This may settle on its own.

However, a bump that becomes:

Painful
Red
Increasingly swollen
Warm
Filled with pus
Persistent

may indicate inflammation or infection and should be assessed by a healthcare professional.

Is Nipple Discharge Always Abnormal?

No.

Nipple discharge can be completely physiological in certain circumstances.

It can occur during:

Pregnancy
Breastfeeding
Early postpartum lactation
Colostrum production
Certain hormonal conditions

Some medications and elevated prolactin levels can also cause nipple discharge.

However, not all nipple discharge is normal.

Certain patterns warrant medical evaluation.

What Nipple Changes Should You Get Checked?

Seek medical evaluation if you notice:

New bloody nipple discharge
Spontaneous discharge from one breast
Persistent clear or watery discharge
Pus-like discharge
A new breast lump
New nipple inversion or retraction
Persistent nipple ulceration
Persistent crusting or eczema-like changes
A new significant change in one nipple
Persistent pain associated with a new breast change

These symptoms do not automatically mean cancer.

There are many benign causes of nipple and breast changes, including infection, hormonal changes, and benign growths such as intraductal papillomas.

However, persistent or unusual changes should be assessed rather than ignored.

Are Montgomery Tubercles a Sign of Pregnancy?

They can become more prominent during pregnancy, but their presence alone does not prove pregnancy.

Hormonal changes during pregnancy can enlarge the Montgomery glands and make the tubercles more visible.

However, many non-pregnant people naturally have prominent Montgomery tubercles.

Therefore:

Visible nipple bumps ≠ definite pregnancy.

Do Montgomery Glands Disappear After Breastfeeding?

They may become less prominent after pregnancy and breastfeeding.

During pregnancy and lactation, hormonal stimulation can make the glands larger and more visible.

After breastfeeding ends and hormone levels return toward their usual state, the glands may become less noticeable.

However, their appearance varies from person to person, and some bumps may remain visible.

Can the Areola Change With Age?

Yes.

The nipple–areola complex can change throughout life.

Changes may occur with:

Puberty
Pregnancy
Breastfeeding
Weight changes
Hormonal fluctuations
Aging

The pigmentation, size, texture, and shape of the areola may therefore change naturally over time.

A gradual change associated with an expected life stage is generally less concerning than a sudden unexplained change.

Does Areola Color Affect Breast Health?

Generally, no.

Areolar pigmentation varies naturally between individuals and is influenced by genetics, hormones, and other factors.

There is no single “healthy” areola color.

Differences in pigmentation are usually normal unless there is a new, persistent, or unusual skin change, such as ulceration, severe scaling, bleeding, or a persistent eczema-like appearance.

Normal vs. Concerning Nipple and Areola Changes

A simple way to think about it is:

Usually normal
Different areola sizes
Different areola colors
Mild breast or nipple asymmetry
Small bumps around the areola
A few hairs around the areola
Montgomery tubercles becoming more visible during pregnancy
Gradual pigmentation changes
Temporary changes associated with breastfeeding
Worth getting checked
A new breast lump
New nipple inversion
Persistent bloody discharge
New spontaneous one-sided discharge
Persistent ulceration
Persistent crusting or eczema-like changes
Significant unexplained skin changes
A painful, red or pus-filled bump
A sudden major change affecting one breast

The key distinction is often whether the feature has always been there or whether it is new and changing.

Frequently Asked Questions About Montgomery Glands and the Areola

What are the little bumps around my nipples?

They are usually Montgomery tubercles, which are the visible parts of Montgomery glands located within the areola. They are normal.

How many Montgomery glands should I have?

There is no single normal number. Studies have reported approximately 4–28 glands per breast, but their number and visibility vary considerably.

Do Montgomery glands produce breast milk?

No. They produce an oily secretion that helps protect and lubricate the nipple–areola complex. Breast milk is produced by the mammary glands deeper inside the breast.

Do bigger areolas mean more breast milk?

No. Areola size does not determine milk production.

Why are my areolas getting darker?

Hormonal changes, particularly during puberty and pregnancy, can increase areolar pigmentation. This is usually normal.

Is it normal to have hair around my nipples?

Yes. A small amount of hair on the areolar skin is common, especially after puberty.

Should I squeeze the bumps around my nipples?

No. Montgomery glands are normal structures, and squeezing them can cause irritation or infection.

Do Montgomery tubercles mean I'm pregnant?

Not necessarily. They can become more prominent during pregnancy, but many people naturally have visible Montgomery tubercles without being pregnant.

Can Montgomery glands get infected?

A gland can occasionally become blocked or inflamed. A painful, red, swollen, or pus-producing bump should be evaluated by a healthcare professional.

Can nipple discharge be normal?

Yes, particularly during pregnancy and breastfeeding. However, new spontaneous one-sided, bloody, persistent clear or pus-like discharge should be medically evaluated.

Does everyone have the same number of Montgomery glands?

No. Their number, size, and visibility vary considerably between individuals.

Conclusion

The nipple–areola complex is a highly specialized part of the breast, and its appearance varies considerably from person to person.

Differences in areola size, shape, and pigmentation, mild nipple asymmetry, visible Montgomery tubercles, and a small amount of hair around the areola can all be normal anatomical variations.

Montgomery glands are particularly important during breastfeeding. Their oily secretions help lubricate and protect the nipple–areola skin, may provide antimicrobial protection, and may release scent cues that help newborns orient toward the breast.

Importantly, the appearance of the areola does not determine breast milk production or breastfeeding success. Milk production depends primarily on the function of the mammary glands, hormonal regulation, and effective milk removal.

Most variations require no treatment. There is no need to squeeze, scrub, or otherwise “clean” Montgomery tubercles.

However, a new or persistent breast or nipple change should not automatically be dismissed as normal. Bloody or spontaneous one-sided discharge, a new lump, nipple retraction, persistent ulceration, unusual skin changes, or a painful infected-looking bump should be evaluated by a healthcare professional.

The most important takeaway is simple:

There is a wide range of normal when it comes to nipples and areolas. What matters most is recognizing what is normal for your own body — and paying attention when something genuinely new or unusual appears.
